title: Jack and Bobby Charlton Win the World Cup
text:
Jack and Bobby Charlton grew up in Ashington, a coal mining town in Northumberland, two years apart in age. Their mother, Cissie, came from a family of footballers and taught them the game. Bobby was the gifted one, signed by Manchester United as a teenager; he survived the Munich air disaster of 1958, which killed eight of his teammates. Jack was a tall, combative defender at Leeds United, a late bloomer who did not play for England until he was nearly thirty.

They were very different men: Bobby reserved and elegant, Jack blunt and outspoken. In 1966, both were in Alf Ramsey's England team for the World Cup on home soil. Bobby scored twice in the semifinal against Portugal, while Jack anchored the defense.

On 30 July 1966, at Wembley Stadium, England beat West Germany 4 to 2 after extra time. When the final whistle blew, Jack sank to his knees, and the brothers embraced. Bobby was named European Footballer of the Year that December.

Later the brothers drifted apart. A family rift, involving their wives and their mother's care, kept them estranged for many years. Jack went on to manage Ireland at two World Cups. He died in 2020, Bobby in 2023.
lesson: Siblings with different temperaments can still win together when they share a goal. Shared triumphs are worth protecting from later quarrels.
people: Bobby Charlton, Jack Charlton, Cissie Charlton, Alf Ramsey
source: 1966 FIFA World Cup records; Jack Charlton, The Autobiography (1996); Bobby Charlton, My England Years (2008)
